summary: Mangalam is our attempt to build a "Palantir for Mars", a unified intelligence and mapping platform that helps astronauts understand, navigate and explore the Martian surface. Focusing on Jezero Crater, Neretva Vallis and the Bright Angel formation, Mangalam brings together NASA's topographical data, orbital imagery, geological information and rover obesrvations to create localized maps for surface exploration as well as scientific investigations. It includes terrain visualization, slope analysis, route planning, hazard assessment and a workspace for scientific investigations. One of our primary features is the integration of our software platform with a hardware robotic reconnaissance and research system either in the form of drones or rovers equipped with cameras, Lidar, GPS, etc, to collect additional surface observations and trasmit them to Mangalam via a web dashboard for integration into local terrain models. By connecting existing planetary data with new robotic observations, Mangalam aims to move beyond conventional Mars mapping and give future exploration crews a more complete picture of where they are going, what they might encounter and what they can investigate.
details:
The idea

We started with a simple question : NASA has collected decades of information about Mars, so why is it still difficult to bring all that information together when planning a specific surface expedition? Mangalam is our answer. We envision it as a Palantir-like operational intelligence platform for Mars ie a place where astronauts can bring together geographical data, scientific observations, robotic intelligence and mission plans instead of having to work across disconnected mapping tools and datasets. Some of our explorations areas are the Jezero Crater, Neretva Vallis and Bright Angel formation. The region offers opportunities to investigate ancient river environments, geological formations and evidence of Mars' watery past.

How it works

Mangalam uses NASA's Mars Global Surveyor MOLA elevation data as its existing terrain foundation. It also includes data connectors for NASA/JPL Mars Trek, USGS planetary geological mapping and the Perseverance raw image data. These resources bring together elevation, orbital imagery, geological units and actual rover photographs into a single map interface. The platform has four main workspaces :

->Mission Map : Astronauts can explore the Martian terrain, inspect coordinates, view elevation and also slope information. They can also exmaine geological layers, mark potential hazards and calculate routes using A* pathfinding algorithm

->Robotics : We are also integrating robotics-based systems for reconnaisance and scientific investigations in the form of drones and rovers which we have built. These systems are equipped with cameras, lidars, positioning sensors, GPS, etc to receive telemetry, timestamped camera images and Lidar observations through a web server. Calibrated robotic measurements can be processed into the separate local terrain maps.

->Science : Crew members can identify investigation sites, formulate research questions, attach photographs, record observations and also maintain scientific records.

->Data & Sources : Mission operators can manage terrain datasets, inspect source information, access available NASA and USGS data connectors and maintain the provenance of imported observations.

Technology

The platform is built using Javascript, HTML, CSS, Node.js and SQLlite Its mapping and mission-planning backend incorporates planetary coordinate handling, elevation and slope analysis, A* pathfinding, REST APIs, WMTS imagery services and persistent mission records. The robotic integration uses an ESP32-based communication interface for telemetry and also suport for camera and lidar observations to add additional things to the maps.

What makes it different (USP)

Most planetary maps help us see Mars. We want Mangalam to help astronauts make sense of it. Its central idea is to connect what we already know of Mars with what robotic explorers can discover next. Existing NASA datasets provide the geographical and scientific foundation while additional robotic observations can progressively expand our understanding of individual exploration areas. Rather than treating a map as a static picture, Mangalam is designed around an evolving record of terrain, observations, scientific targets and mission decisions. It also retains information about where datasets came from and helps to distinguish betwen measured, imported or simulated unverified information.

Conclusion

Our long term vision is to give astronauts a single operational environment/platform from which they can understand their surroundings, plan excursions, plan robotic reconnaissance or investigations and make more informed decisions. Mangalam is currently a research and engineering prototype with hardware demonstration only Earth based using WiFi. It is designed as a foundation for future exploration and we are confident it will achieve that goal.
